answer.evidence: The main body is the sign panel, rows 0-14 and 10 px wide. It is a flat, face-on board. The cream rows 1-3 and the gold line at row 4 belong to the printed design and are not a horizontal surface, because no front-edge line or eave shadow sits under a top band and the silhouette is a plain rectangle with a 1-row outline. The pole in rows 15-27 is a 4 px vertical shaft. The base in rows 28-31 is only 4 rows tall, with a 1-row lighter strip at row 29. That is a rim, not a top surface or ellipse. Nothing in the drawing reads as a top plane, so it is a front elevation.

styleAnswer.evidence: The candidate is a small sign on a pole: an orange/yellow sign head with a dark top band, and a thin dark pole on a base. It measures 13 visible tones per tile, against 6 for bus-shelter, 12 for kiosk and 20 for vending. That is above two of the three references and below only vending-a, which is a much bigger, denser object. Near-flat coverage is 0%, so there are no flat fills. The dark edge pixels are 0% neutral, so the outline is tinted, as in the references (dark material tone). The sign face shows a few shading steps (highlight, light, mid, dark) plus a number glyph, which is a bit fewer than the larger references but suits a thin prop. By eye it sits next to the kiosk and vending pieces without looking thinner or more sticker-like. The pole is slim, but it is cleanly shaded and has a base.
